questions.q: A 6-year-old unvaccinated child presents with a 3-day history of high fever, coryza, conjunctivitis, and a barking cough. On examination, you note small red macules with white centers on the buccal mucosa opposite the premolar teeth. What is the clinical significance of these oral findings?
opts: They indicate secondary bacterial infection requiring immediate antibiotic therapy
They are pathognomonic enanthem (Koplik's spots) appearing 48 hours before the characteristic exanthem
They represent aphthous ulcers from immune complex deposition
They are diagnostic of infectious mononucleosis rather than measles
questions.exp:
Koplik's spots are the pathognomonic enanthem of measles, appearing as tiny bright red macules with 1-2 mm blue-white ('grains of sand') centers on the buccal mucosa, characteristically opposite the premolar teeth. They appear during the prodromal phase, 48 hours prior to the exanthem, making them crucial early diagnostic markers. These spots fade as the characteristic maculopapular rash emerges.
🏰 Palace: Imagine a SAND CASTLE on a RED BEACH with GRAINS OF SAND (Koplik's spots) spilling out 2 days before the MEASLES WAVE crashes ashore behind the child's EARS.

questions.q: A 48-year-old woman with a trichilemmal cyst on her scalp develops sudden pain, warmth, and purulent drainage. What is the most appropriate immediate management?
opts: Complete surgical excision under local anesthesia immediately
Incision and drainage with deferral of excision until inflammation subsides
Topical antibiotic cream without drainage
Observation and reassurance as infection is self-limiting
questions.exp: When a trichilemmal cyst becomes inflamed, painful, or purulent, incision and drainage should be performed to address the infection, but complete excision should be deferred until inflammation has resolved to reduce the risk of wound dehiscence and complications. Complete excision of an actively inflamed cyst is more technically challenging and carries higher morbidity.

questions.q: A patient with suspected bullous pemphigoid requires a biopsy for direct immunofluorescence (DIF) testing. Which fixative medium should be used for the DIF specimen?
opts: 10% neutral buffered formalin, as it is the standard fixative for all skin biopsies
Michel's medium, Zeus medium, or normal saline to preserve immunoglobulins
Alcohol-based fixative for rapid processing
Glutaraldehyde solution for enhanced antigen preservation
questions.exp: DIF specimens must NEVER be placed in formalin, which destroys the immunoglobulins required for diagnostic visualization. Michel's medium, Zeus medium, or normal saline are appropriate transport media that preserve antibody-antigen complexes necessary for accurate immunofluorescence testing.

questions.q: A 6-month-old girl with Goltz syndrome shows clinical features limited to the right side of her body following the lines of Blaschko, while her left side is unaffected. Which genetic mechanism best explains this unilateral distribution pattern in an affected female?
opts: Somatic mosaic PORCN mutation acquired post-zygotically affecting only right-sided embryonic cell lineages
Random X-chromosome inactivation (lyonization) creating functional mosaicism in different body regions
Hemizygous inheritance of the PORCN mutation from an asymptomatic carrier father
Klinefelter syndrome (47,XXY) in combination with a germline PORCN mutation
questions.exp: In females with Focal Dermal Hypoplasia, random X-chromosome inactivation (lyonization) occurs normally during early embryogenesis, creating a mosaic population of cells expressing either the normal or mutant PORCN allele. The distribution of these two cell populations during embryonic migration determines which body areas are affected, resulting in cutaneous lesions that strictly follow the lines of Blaschko. Somatic mosaicism is the mechanism in male survivors; hemizygous inheritance is impossible from fathers (males pass Y to sons); Klinefelter is relevant only for surviving males.
questions.palace: 🏰 Palace: A ROYAL FLIPPER (female X-activation/lyonization) randomly selects which side of the CASTLE MIRROR shows the CURSED REFLECTION—heads right, tails left—drawing BLASCHKO'S STRIPE through the moat.

questions.q: A 5-week-old full-term neonate presents to the emergency department with fever, nuchal rigidity, and irritability. On examination, there is no cutaneous rash or pustules. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis reveals pleocytosis. Which clinical variant of neonatal listeriosis does this presentation most consistent with, and how does it differ from the early-onset form in terms of cutaneous involvement?
opts: Late-onset listeriosis; skin is generally not involved in the initial presentation, unlike early-onset disease which features characteristic pustules
Granulomatosis infantiseptica; skin involvement is absent because the infection targets only meningeal structures
Early-onset listeriosis; meningitis is the hallmark feature, and cutaneous lesions appear only in atypical cases
Late-onset listeriosis; cutaneous petechiae are always present at disease onset in full-term infants
questions.exp: Late-onset neonatal listeriosis is acquired during passage through an infected birth canal or postnatally, characteristically affects healthy full-term infants, and presents weeks after birth as meningitis or meningoencephalitis. Crucially, unlike early-onset disease (granulomatosis infantiseptica), the skin is generally not involved in late-onset disease. Early-onset disease presents at birth or within days with characteristic discrete grey-white papules and pustules.

questions.q: A genetic counselor is reviewing the molecular basis of Cockayne Syndrome with a family. The parents ask why their child's disorder involves problems with DNA repair rather than autoimmune attack. Which gene and molecular pathway defect is the true pathologic target in approximately 80% of Cockayne Syndrome patients?
opts: ERCC8 gene mutation causing defective nucleotide excision repair in non-transcribed DNA strands
ERCC6 gene mutation causing defective Transcription-Coupled Nucleotide Excision Repair (TC-NER) and inability to recover mRNA synthesis after UV exposure
HLA-linked autoimmune target causing anti-melanocyte antibody deposition at the dermal-epidermal junction
BRCA1 gene mutation causing impaired homologous recombination and increased cancer predisposition
questions.exp: ERCC6 (CS-B) mutations account for approximately 80% of Cockayne Syndrome cases and specifically impair Transcription-Coupled Nucleotide Excision Repair (TC-NER), the sub-pathway responsible for removing UV-induced photoproducts from actively transcribing genes. This defect prevents recovery of mRNA synthesis after UV radiation, causing the pathognomonic cellular dysfunction in CS.
questions.hook: 🏰 Palace: ERCC6 is the CASTLE'S CHIEF REPAIR FOREMAN (80% of the workforce)—without him, the TRANSCRIPT WORKERS (mRNA) can't resume their jobs after UV storms, so the whole kingdom ages prematurely from incomplete message delivery.

questions.q: A newborn presents with bluish-red infiltrative papules and nodules at birth. Histopathology reveals dermal extramedullary erythropoiesis with aggregates of nucleated cells and non-nucleated erythrocytes in the reticular dermis. Which pathophysiological mechanism best explains this 'blueberry muffin' lesion?
opts: Autoimmune-mediated destruction of melanocytes leading to pigment loss
Direct microbial invasion triggering severe systemic infectious stress with compensatory fetal hematopoiesis
Deposition of immune complexes in dermal blood vessels causing vasculitis
Aberrant differentiation of dermal fibroblasts into adipocytes
questions.exp: Blueberry muffin lesions represent a non-inflammatory dermal manifestation of extramedullary erythropoiesis—a direct response of the fetal hematopoietic system to severe systemic infectious stress. These are characteristic of TORCH infections and occur as plaque-like aggregates in the reticular dermis, not from immune-mediated damage. The bluish-red appearance reflects the concentration of erythroid precursor cells rather than inflammation.
questions.palace: 🏰 Palace: Picture a NEWBORN BAKING BLUEBERRY MUFFINS in the castle kitchen—the blue berries represent fetal blood cells WORKING OVERTIME in the dermis, stressed and exhausted from fighting invisible infections in the womb.

questions.q: A 6-month-old infant presents with multiple hypomelanotic macules on the trunk and extremities. Genetic testing reveals a de novo mutation in TSC2. Which of the following best explains why this patient is expected to have a more severe phenotype compared to an infant with a TSC1 mutation?
opts: TSC2 encodes hamartin, which has greater interaction with the actin cytoskeleton than tuberin

TSC2 encodes tuberin, a GTPase-activating protein that directly inhibits Rheb-GTP; loss of TSC2 produces more severe mTORC1 hyperactivation and higher rates of intellectual disability and treatment-resistant seizures
TSC2 is located on chromosome 9q34, which is subject to greater rates of somatic recombination than chromosome 16p13.3
TSC2 mutations exclusively cause gonadal mosaicism, leading to multi-organ involvement in offspring
questions.exp: TSC2 encodes tuberin, the GTPase-activating protein that directly suppresses Rheb-GTP and mTORC1 signaling. TSC2 mutations (found in ~70% of sporadic cases) produce significantly more severe disease with higher rates of intellectual disability, treatment-resistant seizures, and renal angiomyolipomas compared to TSC1 mutations. TSC1 encodes hamartin, a scaffold protein that stabilizes tuberin; TSC1 mutations typically yield milder phenotypes.
questions.source: Tuberous Sclerosis Complex (TSC1 TSC2, Hamartin, Tuberin, Ash-Leaf, Shagreen, Koenen)
questions.memory: 🏰 Palace: Picture TUBERIN as a HEAVY BRAKE on a runaway mTOR locomotive at 16p13—when TSC2 is deleted, the brakes EXPLODE and the train CRASHES HARD with seizures and kidney tumors.

questions.q: A 18-month-old boy presents with severe growth retardation, progressive neurological decline, sensorineural hearing loss, and characteristic "bird-like" facies with deep-set eyes and beaked nose. Ophthalmologic examination reveals a salt-and-pepper retinal pattern. Genetic testing identifies mutations in the ERCC6 gene. Which of the following statements about his malignancy risk is most accurate?
opts: He has markedly increased risk of melanoma and non-melanoma skin cancers similar to patients with Xeroderma Pigmentosum
He has absolutely no increased risk of skin cancers despite extreme UV sensitivity because defective TC-NER causes low-level DNA damage lesions to undergo apoptosis rather than accumulate mutations
He will develop multiple basal cell carcinomas by the second decade of life due to cumulative photodamage
His cancer risk depends entirely on HLA genotype and autoimmune status, requiring immunosuppressive therapy to prevent malignant transformation
questions.exp: Cockayne Syndrome Type I patients paradoxically have NO increased malignancy risk despite severe UV photosensitivity because cells accumulating unrepaired DNA damage from defective TC-NER undergo apoptosis, preventing carcinogenic mutation accumulation—unlike XP where mutations accumulate and cause frequent skin cancers. This is a critical distinguishing feature that separates CS from other photosensitive genodermatoses.
questions.hook: 🏰 Palace: Imagine a CANCER HOSPITAL on one side of the castle (XP) packed with tumor patients, but on the OTHER SIDE (CS), apoptotic CELL CORPSES pile up instead—the body chooses DEATH OVER CANCER, preserving the kingdom at the cost of premature aging.

questions.q: A 52-year-old woman presents with multiple firm, skin-colored nodules on her scalp. Clinical examination reveals well-circumscribed, mobile lesions without visible openings. Histopathology shows stratified squamous epithelium lining the cyst wall with abrupt keratinization and absence of a granular layer. What is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Epidermoid cyst
Trichilemmal cyst
Lipoma
Sebaceous cyst with granular layer
questions.exp: The combination of scalp location (90% of trichilemmal cysts occur here), absence of a punctum, and the distinctive histopathologic finding of absent granular layer with abrupt keratinization is pathognomonic for trichilemmal cyst. Epidermoid cysts would show a granular layer and are more common on the face and trunk with potential puncta.

questions.q: A 6-year-old boy presents with multiple dome-shaped, pearly-white papules (3–4 mm) with central umbilication on his trunk and arms. Which molluscum contagiosum virus (MCV) genotype is most likely responsible for this presentation?
opts: MCV-2, which accounts for >90% of childhood infections worldwide
MCV-1, which is responsible for 76–98% of childhood infections globally
MCV-3, which is the most common subtype in immunocompromised children
MCV-4, which exclusively affects children under 10 years of age
questions.exp: MCV-1 is the dominant subtype worldwide, accounting for 76–97% of childhood infections globally and up to 98% of cases in the United States. MCV-2 is predominantly seen in adults (sexually transmitted) and immunosuppressed individuals. MCV-3 and MCV-4 are extremely rare subtypes.
questions.palace: 🏰 Palace: Picture a CHILD playing with a GIANT #1 TROPHY in the castle (MCV-1 dominates childhood). The trophy sparkles with 98 diamonds for USA.

questions.q: A 3-year-old girl with a family history of tuberous sclerosis is found to have a unilateral patch of facial angiofibromas strictly respecting the midline, but no brain lesions, seizures, or systemic hamartomas on imaging. Genetic testing of affected skin shows a TSC1 mutation, but blood germline testing is normal. What is the most likely explanation for this clinical presentation?
opts: This represents NMI-TSC with somatic mosaicism confined to dermal fibroblasts only
The patient has mosaic (segmental) TSC from a postzygotic mutation in TSC1 during embryogenesis; the mutation is localized to the affected skin segment, explaining the absence of systemic disease
This is early-stage familial TSC with incomplete penetrance; systemic manifestations will inevitably develop
The patient has TSC2/PKD1 contiguous gene deletion syndrome with focal skin involvement
questions.exp: Mosaic (segmental) TSC arises from a postzygotic (somatic) mutation during embryogenesis and presents with features strictly localized to a specific body segment, respecting anatomical midlines. When the mutation is isolated to skin, systemic complications are absent because the mutation was not present in other germline tissues during development. This patient's unilateral, midline-respecting angiofibromas with normal blood germline testing and absence of systemic disease are pathognomonic for segmental TSC.
questions.source: Tuberous Sclerosis Complex (TSC1 TSC2, Hamartin, Tuberin, Ash-Leaf, Shagreen, Koenen)
questions.memory: 🏰 Palace: Mosaic TSC is like a HALF-PAINTED CASTLE—the mutation arrived LATE during building (postzygotic), so only ONE WING got the bad blueprint; the rest of the castle is pristine because those workers never got the corrupted plans.

questions.q: A 6-year-old boy presents with symmetric, shiny erythema and superficial scaling on the weight-bearing surfaces of both feet, with characteristic sparing of the interdigital web spaces. What is the pathological mechanism underlying juvenile plantar dermatosis?
opts: Autoimmune blistering directed against hemidesmosomes
Irritant contact dermatitis from a compromised epidermal barrier triggered by humidity-to-dryness transitions in occlusive footwear
Fungal infection of the stratum corneum with dermatophyte overgrowth
Allergic contact dermatitis to rubber and synthetic shoe materials with specific IgE-mediated pathways
questions.exp: Juvenile plantar dermatosis is an irritant contact and frictional dermatitis, not autoimmune or fungal, driven by the physical transition from a humid, macerated environment to rapid drying—exacerbated by hyperhidrosis, occlusive synthetic footwear, and friction. The condition is not mediated by autoantibodies, specific HLA associations, or true allergic mechanisms.

questions.q: A 7-year-old girl with multiple molluscum contagiosum lesions develops an eczematous inflammatory halo surrounding several of the papules. Her mother is concerned about secondary bacterial infection. What does this inflammatory response most accurately represent?
opts: Evidence of bacterial superinfection requiring immediate antibiotic therapy
A pathological progression toward scarring and permanent disfigurement
A robust host immune response (Meyerson's phenomenon) that frequently precedes spontaneous viral clearance
Conversion of classic molluscum to the giant molluscum variant seen only in immunocompromised hosts
questions.exp: Meyerson's phenomenon is the eczematous inflammatory halo around molluscum papules, representing a strong host immune response involving plasmacytoid dendritic cells and cytotoxic T lymphocytes—not bacterial infection. This inflammation typically precedes spontaneous resolution and viral clearance, indicating a favorable prognostic sign.
questions.palace: 🏰 Palace: MEYERSON (a MAYOR) is CELEBRATING inside a HALO of LIGHT in the castle, rejoicing as the immune knights defeat the virus and it disappears—a GOOD sign, not bad.

questions.q: A 22-year-old patient presents with progressive milky-white macules on the dorsal hands and face. Genetic analysis reveals mutations in genes related to innate and adaptive immunity. According to genome-wide association studies, approximately what percentage of vitiligo susceptibility loci are associated with immune-related pathways?
opts: Approximately 50%
Approximately 70%
Approximately 90%
Approximately 100%
questions.exp: GWAS studies have identified approximately 50 susceptibility loci in vitiligo, with approximately 90% of these related to innate and adaptive immunity, while only 10% relate to melanocyte antigens and stress-response pathways. This finding supports the autoimmune theory as the dominant pathogenic mechanism in vitiligo.

questions.q: A 7-year-old girl with a history of atopic dermatitis develops painful fissures on the forefoot and ball of the foot bilaterally, but the toe clefts and arch areas remain completely unaffected. Which histological finding would be most characteristic if a biopsy were performed?
opts: Spongiform pustules with Munro microabscesses in the stratum corneum
Inflammation specifically targeting the acrosyringium and eccrine sweat ducts within a background of mild spongiosis
Dermal fibrosis with loss of elastic fibers and loss of rete ridge architecture
Subepidermal bulla formation with linear IgA deposition at the basement membrane zone
questions.exp: The key distinguishing histological feature of juvenile plantar dermatosis is inflammation specifically localizing around the acrosyringium and eccrine sweat ducts, occurring within a non-specific chronic eczematous background of spongiosis and acanthosis. This eccrine duct-centric inflammation reflects the pathogenic role of maceration and hyperhidrosis in the pathogenesis.

questions.q: A mother presents at 32 weeks gestation with primary genital HSV infection. What is the estimated risk of vertical transmission to her neonate if she delivers vaginally during active viral shedding?
opts: Less than 1%
questions.exp: Primary maternal genital HSV infection acquired near delivery (third trimester) carries a catastrophic 30–50% transmission risk due to high viral shedding and absence of protective transplacental maternal antibodies. This contrasts sharply with recurrent maternal herpes, which carries <1–3% risk.

questions.q: A 45-year-old woman presents with progressive leg symptoms including aching, heaviness, and throbbing, aggravated by prolonged standing. Examination reveals tortuous veins >3 mm on the medial calf with mild dependent edema but no skin changes. According to the CEAP classification, what is her clinical grade?
opts: C1
C2
C3
C4a
questions.exp: The patient has varicose veins (≥3 mm) on examination, which corresponds to C2 in the CEAP classification. C1 includes only telangiectasias (<1 mm) or reticular veins (1–3 mm), while C3 requires edema without skin changes—but this patient has the varicose veins as the primary finding. C4a includes pigmentation or eczematous changes, which are not present.

questions.q: A 2-day-old infant is found to have the classic pathognomonic triad of chorioretinitis, hydrocephalus, and intracranial calcifications. Histopathology of a skin biopsy shows subacute histiolymphocytic vasculitis with crescent-shaped trophozoites containing a prominent centrally-placed nucleus within macrophage cytoplasm. What is the causative organism?
opts: Treponema pallidum
Toxoplasma gondii
Varicella-zoster virus
Cytomegalovirus
questions.exp: Congenital toxoplasmosis is caused by Toxoplasma gondii, an obligate intracellular protozoan that forms tissue cysts. The pathognomonic histological finding is crescent-shaped trophozoites with a centrally-placed nucleus within macrophages, often in pseudocysts. The classic clinical triad of chorioretinitis, hydrocephalus, and intracranial calcifications (tram-track pattern) is uniquely characteristic of congenital toxoplasmosis.
questions.palace: 🏰 Palace: A CRESCENT MOON (Toxoplasma's shape) hangs above the castle, shining light through THREE CASTLE TOWERS—one for eyes (chorioretinitis), one for brain water (hydrocephalus), one for train tracks in stone (calcifications). Inside the castle moat, a CROISSANT-SHAPED PARASITE hides in the MACROPHAGE'S POCKET.

questions.q: A 2-day-old premature neonate is brought to the NICU with severe lethargy, hepatosplenomegaly, and a generalized eruption of discrete 1–2 mm grey-white papules and pustules with red margins predominantly on the back. The mother reports meconium-stained amniotic fluid. Which bacterial virulence factor is responsible for the pathogenesis of this condition?
opts: Lipopolysaccharide (LPS) endotoxin on the bacterial cell wall
Internalin A, a bacterial surface protein that binds host receptors to induce bacterial uptake into non-phagocytic cells
Pathogenic autoantibodies directed against desmoglein-1
Heat-labile enterotoxin produced by the organism
questions.exp: Listeria monocytogenes utilizes internalin A as a specific bacterial surface protein required to bind host cell receptors and induce the bacterium's own uptake into non-phagocytic host cells. This is the key molecular mechanism of pathogenesis. The clinical presentation of meconium-stained amniotic fluid, prematurity, and discrete cutaneous pustules with red margins is classic for granulomatosis infantiseptica (early-onset neonatal listeriosis).

questions.q: A skin biopsy from a child with suspected measles reveals multinucleated keratinocytes in the epidermis along with superficial perivascular lymphocytic infiltrate and mild spongiosis. Which of the following cellular structures are responsible for this pathognomonic histological finding?
opts: Langerhans cells undergoing apoptosis triggered by viral dyskeratosis
Syncytial giant cells formed by viral-mediated fusion of keratinocytes
Eosinophilic microabscesses characteristic of dermatitis herpetiformis
Palisading histiocytes surrounding areas of necrosis
questions.exp:
The pathognomonic histological finding in measles is the presence of multinucleated keratinocytes (syncytial giant cells) in the epidermis, formed by viral-mediated fusion of cells. These Warthin-Finkeldey cells are also found in lymph nodes and reticuloendothelial tissues. The epidermis additionally shows non-specific superficial perivascular lymphocytic infiltrate, mild spongiosis, papillary edema, and dyskeratosis.
🏰 Palace: Picture a MULTIPLAYER VIDEO GAME where VIRUS PLAYERS FUSE KERATINOCYTES together into GIANT MULTI-HEADED MONSTERS (syncytial giant cells) running wild through the CASTLE EPIDERMIS.

questions.q: A 45-year-old patient presents with a suspicious pigmented lesion on the back measuring 8 mm. Clinical examination raises concern for melanoma. Which biopsy modality is most appropriate?
opts: Shave biopsy for quick diagnosis and minimal scarring
Excisional biopsy with complete removal and margin assessment
Punch biopsy to minimize tissue removal
Incisional biopsy to preserve surrounding skin
questions.exp: Excisional biopsy is the gold standard for suspected melanoma because it allows simultaneous diagnosis and definitive treatment with complete margin assessment. Shave biopsy is absolutely contraindicated in melanoma as it compromises Breslow depth measurement, which is critical for staging and prognosis.

questions.q: A dermatosurgeon is planning treatment for a 38-year-old patient with telangiectasias and reticular veins on the lower extremities. Color duplex ultrasonography confirms no saphenous reflux. Which treatment modality is most appropriate as the primary intervention?
opts: Endovenous laser ablation (EVLA)
Sclerotherapy with liquid or foam sclerosant
Saphenofemoral ligation and stripping
Ambulatory phlebectomy alone
questions.exp: Sclerotherapy is the primary treatment for telangiectasias, reticular veins, and non-saphenous varicose veins, achieved through targeted injection of a sclerosant to destroy the endothelium. EVLA and saphenofemoral ligation are reserved for incompetent saphenous trunks, which are absent in this patient. Phlebectomy is combined with endovenous ablation rather than used alone for these small vessels.

questions.q: A patient with vitiligo experiences significant physical stress, which triggers heat-shock protein (HSP 70i) production by melanocytes. How does this stress response contribute to the pathogenesis of vitiligo?
opts: HSP 70i directly blocks melanin production within melanocytes
HSP 70i translocates to the cell surface and releases TRAIL, sensitizing the innate immune response and priming cellular immunity via dendritic cells
HSP 70i increases E-cadherin expression, promoting melanocyte migration to lesional sites
HSP 70i inhibits CD8+ T cell activation, preventing autoimmune destruction
questions.exp: Stress-induced heat-shock proteins (HSP 70i) translocate to the melanocyte cell surface and release TRAIL (TNF alpha-related apoptosis-inducing ligand), which sensitizes the innate immune response and stimulates dendritic cells to prime cellular immunity. This is a key mechanism linking stress to the activation of autoimmune destruction of melanocytes in vitiligo.

questions.q: A 3-day-old female neonate presents with linear, punctate areas of skin atrophy with characteristic 'ice pick-like' depressions following a streaky distribution on her trunk and extremities. Genetic testing reveals a loss-of-function mutation in the PORCN gene on chromosome Xp11.23. Which of the following molecular mechanisms underlies the primary dermal pathology in this condition?
opts: Disrupted Wnt signaling pathway leading to failure of dermal connective tissue formation
Autoimmune destruction of dermal fibroblasts mediated by circulating anti-basement membrane antibodies
Defective type IV collagen synthesis due to mutations in COL4A genes
Excessive apoptosis of melanocytes triggered by HLA-associated immune complex deposition
questions.exp: Focal Dermal Hypoplasia is caused by PORCN gene mutations that impair the PORCN protein's ability to regulate membrane targeting and secretion of Wnt proteins, which are essential for normal embryonic development of mesodermal and ectodermal tissues. This disrupted Wnt signaling leads to profound dermal thinning and the characteristic cribriform atrophy. FDH is NOT an autoimmune or immunobullous disorder, so antibody-mediated and HLA-associated mechanisms are not operative.
questions.palace: 🏰 Palace: Picture WORMS (Wnt) crawling through a PORCH (PORCN) on Xp11's castle wall—when the porch breaks, dermal bricks crumble and fat bulges up like a herniated cushion through the floor.

questions.q: A 10-day-old neonate presents with grouped vesicles on an erythematous base affecting the scalp at the fetal monitor electrode site, along with keratoconjunctivitis and oral ulceration. There is no evidence of CNS or systemic involvement. What is the mortality rate for this clinical presentation if appropriately treated?
questions.exp: Skin-Eye-Mouth (SEM) disease presents with vesicles strictly limited to skin, conjunctiva, and oral mucosa without CNS or visceral organ involvement. The mortality rate for isolated SEM disease is 0%; however, untreated disease can rapidly progress to disseminated or CNS infection.
